bp: Many knowledge-heavy applications now ask a language model to answer only after it has looked up outside material. That pattern, retrieval-augmented generation, is useful because the answer can be tied to documents, tables, graphs, or other records instead of coming only from the model's stored habits. This tutorial starts from a harder fact: real knowledge is rarely one flat pile of passages. A business database has tables and columns. A social system has people and links. A long report has sections inside sections. Each shape tells the system something about how evidence should be found and trusted. The practical need is therefore not just to fetch more context, but to build answer systems that understand the structure of the knowledge source and the risks that structure creates. The paper serves practitioners who need a map of this whole lifecycle, from structured evidence to final answers and safety defenses.
wh: The hard part is that structure is both helpful and dangerous. A table can answer precise questions, but only if the system respects rows, columns, and schema meanings. A social network can reveal nearby evidence, but links may spread misleading influence. A document tree can keep section context, but flattening it may separate a sentence from the heading that explains it. A plain retrieval system usually treats all stored material as comparable chunks, then ranks them by surface match to the question. That breaks when the useful clue is in a relation, a hierarchy, or a typed field rather than in matching words. Safety makes the problem sharper. In high-stakes settings, a bad retrieval path can support a plausible but wrong answer, and an attacker may exploit the structure itself by planting misleading records, links, or passages. The tutorial exists because these issues are scattered across different communities and designs.
naive: A smart beginner would build one general pipeline: cut every knowledge source into text snippets, search for snippets that resemble the user's question, paste the top ones into the model, and ask for an answer. This can work for simple factual lookup. It fails when the knowledge source carries meaning in its form. A database column name, a graph edge, or a document section boundary is not just extra decoration; it changes what a retrieved fact means. The same flat pipeline also misses structure-specific attacks. Poisoned table entries, misleading graph links, or malicious text hidden in a document branch can steer the answer while still looking relevant.
ap: The tutorial's central move is to treat retrieval-augmented generation as a structured knowledge problem rather than as text search followed by fluent writing. It surveys the full lifecycle of these systems and asks, at each stage, what kind of object the system is handling. If the outside knowledge is tabular, the design must preserve field meanings and schema relations. If it is a social network or knowledge graph, the design must reason over linked entities and decide which paths carry useful evidence. If it is a document tree, the design must keep parent-child context and section boundaries. The tutorial also puts safety into the same structural view. It does not treat attacks and defenses as an afterthought; it asks how the shape of the source changes what can go wrong and what protection should inspect.
mech: The mechanism described by the abstract is a teaching workflow, so the moving parts are design principles rather than one new algorithm. The input is a knowledge-intensive task plus an outside knowledge collection whose shape matters: tables with schemas, social networks with links, document trees with hierarchy, or other structured sources. First, the system must represent that source without erasing the signals carried by its form. A table needs names, fields, and relations between fields; a network needs nodes and links; a tree needs section order and nesting. Second, the retriever must choose evidence using the right unit. It may need a row, a linked neighborhood, a path, a subtree, or a passage with its heading, not just a loose text fragment. Third, the generator receives selected evidence and turns it into a downstream task solution, such as an answer or decision support. Fourth, safety checks ask whether the selected evidence can be trusted, whether the structure was manipulated, and whether the generated response is overconfident. The output of the tutorial is not a single prediction; it is a structured map of canonical designs, specialized designs for different knowledge forms, and attack and defense strategies.
math: The main mathematical idea is structured evidence selection under uncertainty. In plain terms, the system has many possible witnesses, and it must decide which witnesses deserve to shape an answer. With a table, the mathematical object is a set of records organized by fields; comparison means matching the question to the right fields and values while preserving how columns constrain one another. With a graph, the object is a set of nodes joined by links; the key question is how far evidence should travel along links before nearby help becomes distant noise. With a document tree, the object is a nested order; a child passage may depend on its parent heading, so removing hierarchy can change meaning. Ranking appears because only a small amount of evidence can be placed before the generator, so candidates must be ordered by usefulness and risk. Probability enters as disciplined uncertainty: the system should notice when evidence is incomplete, conflicting, or suspicious rather than treating a fluent answer as proof. Security adds an adversarial version of the same math: a record is not merely useful or useless, but may be crafted to redirect retrieval, pollute a path, or cause unsafe generation.
dots: This paper sits in the retrieval-augmented generation family, where many 2026 papers ask how an answer system should choose and govern outside evidence. Its distinctive role is broad and structural: instead of focusing only on conflict, confidence, document quality, graph search, or cost, it explains how those concerns change when the source is a table, network, or tree. It connects directly to information retrieval because the system must select a small useful set from a large store. It connects to graph reasoning because social networks and linked knowledge make evidence travel through relationships. It connects to ranking because retrieved candidates must be ordered before the generator can use them. It also connects to security and privacy-adjacent work because high-stakes use turns retrieval into an attack surface. The abstract frames the contribution as a tutorial that organizes fragmented work into a lifecycle view, not as a paper claiming one new experimental result.
ww: The approach works as a conceptual guide because it starts from what the evidence is made of. A flat text-only view forces every source through the same narrow doorway, so important constraints disappear before retrieval even begins. A structural view keeps those constraints available. In a table, field names prevent the system from confusing one kind of value with another. In a graph, links let the system look for supporting or neighboring facts when one isolated record is too thin. In a document tree, hierarchy keeps a paragraph tied to the section that gives it scope. These structures also tell defenders where to look. If an answer depends on a suspicious graph path, a strange table cell, or a document branch that carries hidden instructions, the safety problem has a concrete location. The gain is not magic accuracy; it is better bookkeeping over evidence, so retrieval, generation, and safety checks can use the same map of how knowledge is organized.
po: The payoff is a rigorous teaching map for people building retrieval-augmented systems on real structured knowledge. According to the abstract, the tutorial covers the full lifecycle, canonical designs, specialized principles for different knowledge structures, applications, and security attack and defense strategies. That buys a more disciplined way to decide how to model tables, networks, and document trees before using them to support generated answers. It also helps make safety specific: the system can ask what risks belong to this structure instead of applying one generic checklist to every knowledge source.
limits: The abstract describes a six-hour tutorial, so it does not prove a new method, report controlled results, or show that one design is best across all settings. Its claims depend on the surveyed work being representative and on practitioners being able to map their own data into the structural categories discussed. The structural view also assumes that schemas, links, and hierarchies are meaningful and available. If they are stale, incomplete, noisy, or deliberately manipulated, structure can mislead as much as it helps. The abstract mentions high-stakes safety, but it cannot by itself establish deployment readiness for medical, financial, legal, or security systems.
